Most of the difficulties of keeping a model in production are not technical. Practitioner surveys and case studies of machine learning deployments agree that the hardest problems lie at the **boundaries between teams**: agreeing on requirements, negotiating data quality, and integrating the model into an existing system [@amershi2019se4ml; @nahar2022collaboration; @paleyes2022challenges]. APE coding is no exception. This chapter describes two answers that proved decisive: a **business data scientist** who is the point of contact for the model, and a **qualification platform** that matches production.

## Three teams around one model

Three teams share responsibility for the model, each with its own constraints:

| Team | Owns | Main concern |
|---|---|---|
| Business team (Sirene register) | The classification, the coding rules, the manual coding teams | Quality of the APE code and workload of the coders |
| IT production teams | The register's information system and the production infrastructure | Availability, security, change control |
| Data science team (SSP Lab) | The training pipeline, the libraries, the development platform | Methods, tools, model quality |

: Teams involved in APE coding. {#tbl-teams}

Without someone who belongs to the business side **and** understands the model, each question crosses team boundaries. Is a drop in the automation rate a drift or a seasonal effect? Is this reported error a one-off or a pattern? May a new model go to production? Those questions then wait, or get answered by whoever is closest, not by whoever should decide.

## The business data scientist as point of contact {#sec-business-ds}

### Why a dedicated role

The literature on machine learning in organisations describes the role names and responsibilities around a model in production [@kreuzberger2023mlops]. It also documents the benefits of placing data scientists **within** the business teams they serve, close to the domain and its decisions [@stelmaszak2023embedded]. The AIML4OS framework, written for official statistics, makes it a recommendation: every model in production should have a named owner [@aiml4os2025, ch. 3].

For APE coding, this owner is a **data scientist placed in the business team**. They are distinct from the innovation team that built the first models. They speak both languages. They know the classification and the coders' work, and they can read a risk–coverage curve, run a training job and review a pull request.

### Responsibilities

| Area | The business data scientist… |
|---|---|
| Requirements | Translates business needs into model requirements: target accuracy $p^*$, acceptable manual workload, codes that must never be wrong |
| Annotation | Organises the annotation campaigns and the golden set: sampling, guidelines, the expert teams' schedule |
| Business feedback | Collects reported errors, sorts one-off errors from patterns, and turns patterns into [rules](data.qmd#sec-rules) validated by experts |
| Retraining | Runs the [retraining protocol](retraining.qmd) and signs off the [quality gates](retraining.qmd#sec-gates) |
| Monitoring | Gives a first analysis of [monitoring](monitoring.qmd) alerts and decides whether they need action |
| Release | Is the interlocutor of the IT production teams for every model release, from qualification to rollback |
| Communication | Reports on quality to management and to users of the APE code |

: Responsibilities of the business data scientist. {#tbl-business-ds}

The data science team stays responsible for the **tools**: libraries, pipelines, development platform. The business data scientist is responsible for the **model as a service to the business**. This separation lets the innovation team move on to other projects without leaving the model without an owner.

### What it takes

The role works only if a few conditions hold:

- **time**: retraining, annotation and monitoring are recurring work, not a side task;
- **access**: the same development platform and the same repositories as the data science team;
- **skills**: Python, Git, statistics, and knowledge of the classification;
- **a mandate**: authority to decide on releases, within rules agreed with the business and IT teams.

## A qualification platform that matches production {#sec-qualification-platform}

### The gap between development and production

The model is developed and trained on SSP Cloud, an open data science platform with GPUs and internet access (see [Architecture](architecture.qmd)). It runs in production on INSEE's internal infrastructure: CPU only, no internet access, strict resource limits and change control. Anything that differs between the two environments can break a release, or change the model's behaviour without anyone noticing:

- a library version that differs, and changes the preprocessing or the numerical results;
- a resource that the model downloads at start-up, unavailable in a closed network;
- a latency or memory footprint measured on a development machine, not on the production CPU;
- a configuration difference in the way the API is exposed to the register.

### What "iso-production" means

The **qualification platform** removes this gap. It reproduces production as closely as possible:

- the same runtime: base image, Python and library versions, CPU-only builds;
- the same resources: CPU and memory limits, number of replicas;
- the same network constraints: no internet access, dependencies served from the internal repository manager;
- the same deployment mechanism and the same configuration as production.

### What is measured there

Each candidate model goes through the same series of checks before release (see [Retraining protocol](retraining.qmd#sec-preprod)):

- **latency** of unit calls (median, p95, p99) and **throughput** in batch mode, under a realistic load;
- **memory footprint** and **start-up time**;
- **online/offline parity**: the served model must reproduce the offline predictions on the test golden set exactly;
- **robustness**: malformed or unexpected inputs must be rejected cleanly, not crash the service.

These are the [non-functional metrics](evaluation.qmd#sec-eval-nonfunctional) of the evaluation. They are only meaningful here.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-qualification
%%| fig-cap: "From development to production."
flowchart LR
  DEV["Development and training<br/>(SSP Cloud: GPU, internet)"] --> REG[("MLflow<br/>registry")]
  REG --> QUAL["Qualification platform<br/>(iso-production: CPU, closed network)"]
  QUAL -->|"latency, memory,<br/>parity, robustness"| GO{"Go / no-go"}
  GO -->|"no"| DEV
  GO -->|"yes"| PROD["Production<br/>(internal infrastructure)"]
```

### Who does what

| Step | Data science team | Business data scientist | IT production / architects |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model artifact and test suite | Provides | Reviews | — |
| Qualification platform | Uses | Uses | Provides and maintains |
| Go / no-go | Advises | Decides | Checks the operational criteria |
| Release and rollback | — | Requests | Executes |

: Sharing of responsibilities around qualification. {#tbl-qualification-raci}

## Open challenges

- **Sustaining annotation.** The golden set needs a small but continuous annotation effort from business experts, in competition with their daily coding work.
- **Skills and continuity.** A single business data scientist is a single point of failure. The role needs backup and documentation.
- **Keeping the platforms aligned.** Every change to production (base image, resource limits, network rules) has to be carried over to the qualification platform, or qualification stops meaning anything.
